Black-footed albatross chicks emerge at an initial body mass that reflects significant investment during the incubation period. Field measurements at Midway Atoll indicate that pipping chicks have a wet weight of approximately 286 grams [Ww0 = approximately 286 grams], a value that represents the residual mass after the yolk reserves have been partially consumed during the latter stages of embryonic development. This neonatal mass is modest relative to the eventual adult size, which for females asymptotes near 2990 grams [Wwi = 2990 grams], placing the species among the smaller of the North Pacific albatrosses. Male Black-footed albatrosses tend to be slightly larger, with the ultimate wet weight for males recorded at approximately 3400 grams [Wwi = approximately 3400 grams], a dimorphism consistent with the pattern observed in other procellariiform seabirds where sexual size differences facilitate niche partitioning during foraging. The incubation period, measured at the typical egg temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], lasts for approximately 65 days [ab = approximately 65 days], a duration comparable to that of the closely related Laysan albatross. This extended incubation reflects the slow developmental pace characteristic of pelagic seabirds that invest heavily in a single offspring per breeding attempt.

The transition from adulthood to senescence unfolds over an exceptionally long period in this species, consistent with the life-history strategy of long-lived seabirds. Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species (39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]), the maximum recorded longevity for Black-footed albatross reaches approximately 15,366 days (approximately 15366 days) [am = approximately 15366 days], which translates to a lifespan in excess of four decades for those individuals that survive the high mortality of the early juvenile years. This extreme longevity is associated with a markedly delayed reproductive schedule. The time since birth at first brood in this species is approximately 1,825 days [tR = approximately 1,825 days], meaning that individuals typically do not attempt to breed until they are roughly five years of age. at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]Such a protracted prereproductive period is typical of albatrosses, which require several years to master the complex foraging skills necessary to provision a chick and to establish a stable nesting territory within dense breeding colonies. Delaying reproduction in this way allows young birds to accumulate body condition and experience.

Sexual maturation, defined as the attainment of gonadal competence, precedes actual breeding by a substantial interval. At a body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 420 days [tp = approximately 420 days], a value that indicates individuals become physiologically capable of reproduction during their second year of life. However, social and experiential constraints prevent most birds from capitalizing on this early gonadal readiness; competition for mates and nest sites on crowded islands means that successful breeding is typically deferred by several more years. This decoupling between physiological puberty and first successful reproduction is a hallmark of long-lived colonial seabirds. The post-fledging period is similarly protracted. At the same thermal regime of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the time since birth at fledging is approximately 140 days [tx = approximately 140 days], meaning that young birds depart the nest at about four and a half months of age. At this stage, fledglings weigh considerably less than adults and depend on stored lipid reserves as they learn to forage independently over the open ocean.

Reproductive output in Black-footed albatross is constrained by the energetic demands of producing a single, large, slow-developing offspring. Under thermoneutral conditions at 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the maximum reproduction rate is extraordinarily low, with females producing at most a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically raising only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. This annual reproductive effort represents a considerable investment given that the egg alone may constitute roughly ten percent of the female's body mass. The wet weight at birth after the pipping process is recorded at 182.5 grams [Wwb = 182.5 grams], a value that accounts for the weight of the hatchling after the absorption of remaining yolk and the loss of eggshell mass. Hatchlings are entirely dependent on parental provisioning for the first several weeks, receiving meals of regurgitated squid, fish eggs, and crustaceans. The slow growth rate of the nestling reflects both the low energy density of the diet and the inherent metabolic constraints of a species adapted to a pelagic existence.

Foraging ecology and migratory behavior further illuminate the life-history constraints operating on this species. Black-footed albatrosses are wide-ranging foragers that traverse vast expanses of the North Pacific, traveling thousands of kilometers during a single provisioning trip. This extreme foraging range imposes a fundamental energetic trade-off: parents must balance the time spent searching for prey against the need to return frequently to the nest to feed a rapidly growing chick. The distant foraging grounds, often located along frontal zones and upwelling regions, provide a diet dominated by flying squid and lanternfish, prey items that are lipid-rich but patchily distributed. Tracking studies have revealed that adults shift their foraging effort in response to oceanographic conditions, preferentially targeting cooler, more productive waters during the chick-rearing period. The species' low reproductive rate and delayed maturity are therefore tightly coupled with the unpredictability of pelagic food resources and the high energetic cost of flight. These ecological pressures have shaped one of the most extreme slow-paced life histories among seabirds, where a single egg per year and decades-long reproductive lifespan represent the optimal evolutionary solution to a challenging marine environment.
